caption:
Was the Cardiff Giant real? No. It was carved from a block of gypsum in a Chicago workshop, buried in a farm field, and dug up a year later on cue.

George Hull, a New York tobacconist and a skeptic, lost an argument at a Methodist revival meeting about the verse in Genesis saying giants once lived on Earth. He decided to prove how easily people could be fooled.

In 1868 he had a 10-foot-4½-inch block quarried at Fort Dodge, Iowa, telling the workmen it was for a Lincoln monument. Sculptors in Chicago hung quilts to muffle the sound of carving. The figure was shaped to imitate Hull's own body. He consulted a geologist, learned hair would not petrify, and left the giant hairless. Its skin was beaten with steel knitting needles set in a board to fake pores, then washed with sulphuric acid to age the stone.

It was buried behind his cousin William Newell's barn in November 1868. On 16 October 1869 hired well-diggers found it. Newell charged fifty cents for a fifteen-minute look; three to five hundred people came a day.

Yale's Othniel C. Marsh called it "a most decided humbug" — fresh tool marks on soluble gypsum. Cornell's first president noted there was no sensible reason to dig a well in that spot. Hull sold his interest for $23,000. P. T. Barnum was refused at $50,000 and had a copy modelled in wax, then exhibited it as the real one. Syndicate head David Hannum, watching people queue for Barnum's fake, said "There's a sucker born every minute" — a line usually misattributed to Barnum.

Hull confessed on 10 December 1869. Both giants were declared fakes in court on 2 February 1870. Still unresolved: whether the Chicago stonecutter who took the job knew what he was making.

Images: a Bain News Service negative of the giant; an 1869 Popular Graphic Arts lithograph; and both sides of an 1873 stereocard of Cardiff Glen, Iowa, from the New York Public Library.
